title: Exploring Enough: A Small Reward Near By, a Large One Down a Corridor, and Values That Start Optimistic

questions.question: Why can a Q-learner settle for a worse reward than the best?
options: It only learns the value of moves it makes, and it keeps making the moves its table already rates highest
Its table cannot hold large values
It always takes the shortest path
questions.explanation: What it never tries it never learns about.

questions.question: With a tenth of the moves random, how often did the learner reach the large goal, and what did its greedy policy return?
questions.explanation: The greedy moves pull a random walk back to the lure before it gets down the corridor.

questions.question: With the table started at 20 and no random moves, what happened?
options: It went to the small goal
It reached the large goal 1970 times and its greedy policy returned 4
questions.explanation: Every untried move looked worth 20, so it tried them all, and found the corridor.

questions.question: With half the moves random, the learner reached the large goal 27 times. What did its greedy policy return?
options: 1: found too seldom to overtake the lure
questions.explanation: More random moves reach further, and the learner behaves at random that much more while it learns.

questions.question: What does starting the values high (optimism) do?
options: It makes the learner reckless for ever
It makes every untried move look best until it has been tried, so exploration is systematic
It removes the need for a reward
questions.explanation: Each tried move is pulled down to what it gave; untried ones stay high and get their turn.

questions.question: Why is optimism dangerous on a real robot without anything else?
options: Trying every move once includes the moves that hurt the robot
questions.explanation: It must be combined with a shield that refuses known dangerous moves (39-09).
